question: A class has 25 pupils. 15 of them are in the football club (F), 12 are in the chess club (C), and 5 are in both clubs. How many pupils are in neither club?
hint: Count the pupils who are in at least one club. Is anybody counted twice?
solution: Adding 15 and 12 counts the 5 pupils in both clubs twice, so 15 + 12 - 5 = 22 pupils are in at least one club. That leaves 25 - 22 = 3 pupils in neither.

A.text: 22 is how many pupils are in at least one club.

B.text: 5 is how many are in both clubs, copied from the question.

D.text: The 5 pupils in both clubs were taken away twice, so 17 seemed to be in a club instead of 22.

E.text: Only the chess players were taken away; the footballers who do not play chess were left in.

question: Every child in a group likes apples, pears or both. 18 of the children like apples (A), 14 like pears (P), and 7 like both fruits. How many children are in the group?
hint: Which children were counted with the apples and again with the pears?
solution: 18 + 14 = 32 counts the 7 children who like both fruits twice. Taking them away once gives 32 - 7 = 25 children.

B.text: 32 counts each child who likes both fruits twice, once with each fruit.

C.text: 11 is how many like apples but not pears.

D.text: 7 is the number who like both fruits, copied from the question.

E.text: 39 adds the 7 who like both instead of taking them away.

question: A class of 30 children had a free afternoon, and each child went to at least one of two places: the museum (M) or the zoo (Z). 20 children went to the museum and 16 went to the zoo. How many went to both places?
hint: What does adding the two visits give you, and why is it more than 30?
solution: Adding the visits gives 20 + 16 = 36, but there are only 30 children. The 36 - 30 = 6 extra visits belong to children who went to both places.

A.text: 36 is where the adding stops; the 30 children still had to be taken away from it.

B.text: 4 is the museum group minus the zoo group, which says nothing about the overlap.

C.text: 10 children went only to the zoo, not to both places.

D.text: 16 is the zoo group, copied from the question.

question: In a group of 20 children, 12 have a dog (D) and 10 have a cat (C). What is the smallest number of children who could have both a dog and a cat?
hint: Try to keep the dog owners and the cat owners apart. How many children would you need for that?
solution: Keeping the two groups apart would need 12 + 10 = 22 children, but there are only 20. So at least 22 - 20 = 2 children have both, and 2 is possible: 10 with only a dog, 8 with only a cat and 2 with both.

A.text: 0 forgets there are only 20 children, too few for 12 and 10 to stay apart.

C.text: 10 is the largest number who could have both, not the smallest.

D.text: 22 adds the dog and cat owners, so a child with both pets is counted twice and the sum is more than the whole group.

E.text: 8 is the number of children with no dog, not with both pets.

question: There are 30 pupils in a class. 18 of them like maths (M) and 21 like art (A). At most how many pupils could like neither subject?
hint: When are the most pupils left out of both groups: when the groups overlap a little, or a lot?
solution: The fewest pupils like at least one subject when all 18 maths fans also like art. Then only the 21 art fans like anything, and 30 - 21 = 9 like neither. With less overlap, more pupils like something, so 9 is the most.

A.text: 0 is the fewest who could like neither, not the most.

B.text: 12 = 30 - 18 takes away only the maths fans, and 3 of those 12 still like art.

C.text: 39 adds the two groups, which counts every pupil who likes both subjects twice.

E.text: 21 is the number of art fans, copied from the question.

question: Each of the 40 pupils in a year learns English, German or both. 28 pupils learn English and 19 learn German. How many learn exactly one of the two languages?
hint: First find how many pupils learn both languages.
solution: 28 + 19 = 47 is 7 more than the 40 pupils, so 7 learn both. Then 28 - 7 = 21 learn only English and 19 - 7 = 12 learn only German, which makes 21 + 12 = 33.

A.text: 40 counts every pupil, the 7 who learn both languages as well.

B.text: 47 is 28 + 19, which counts the pupils who learn both languages twice.

D.text: 7 pupils learn both languages, not exactly one.

E.text: 12 learn only German; the 21 who learn only English were missed.

question: There are 32 pupils in Year 6. 15 sing in the choir, 13 act in the drama group and 12 paint in the art group. 5 are in both choir and drama, 4 in both choir and art, and 3 in both drama and art. These numbers include the 2 pupils who are in all three groups. How many pupils are in none of the groups?
hint: Add the three groups, then deal with the pupils counted more than once. How many times is a pupil in all three groups counted by the end?
solution: 15 + 13 + 12 = 40 counts each pupil in two groups twice, so take away 5 + 4 + 3 = 12. A pupil in all three groups was counted three times and taken away three times, so add the 2 back: 40 - 12 + 2 = 30 pupils are in some group. That leaves 32 - 30 = 2.

A.text: 4 forgets to add back the 2 pupils in all three groups, who were taken away with every pair.

B.text: 6 takes the 2 pupils in all three groups away once more, as if the pairs had not counted them.

C.text: 9 uses only the choir and drama: 32 - (15 + 13 - 5) = 9. The art group was never counted.

D.text: 0 assumes every pupil is in some group, but the question never says so.

question: A team has 10 pupils. 7 of them can swim, 8 can skate and 9 can ride a bike. At least how many pupils on the team must be able to do all three?
hint: Count the pupils who cannot do each thing. How many of them can there be at most?
solution: 3 pupils cannot swim, 2 cannot skate and 1 cannot ride a bike. Even if these are all different pupils, only 3 + 2 + 1 = 6 miss something. The other 10 - 6 = 4 can do all three, and 4 is possible when the six are all different.

B.text: 7 is the most who could do all three, not the fewest.

C.text: 5 = 7 + 8 - 10 is the fewest who can both swim and skate; the bike riders were never brought in.

D.text: 0 forgets there are only 10 pupils, so the three groups have to overlap.

E.text: 24 adds the three groups, which gives more than the 10 pupils.

question: A year has 50 pupils. 32 of them read comics (C) and 25 read magazines (M). Twice as many pupils read both as read neither. How many pupils read neither?
hint: Try a number for those who read neither, and check whether the total comes out as 50.
solution: If n pupils read neither, then 2n read both, and 32 + 25 - 2n = 57 - 2n read at least one. Together 57 - 2n + n = 57 - n makes 50, so n = 7. Check: 14 read both, 43 read at least one, and 43 + 7 = 50.

C.text: 18 = 50 - 32 counts everyone who skips comics, but some of them read magazines.

D.text: 25 is the number of magazine readers, copied from the question.

E.text: 57 adds the two groups, so the pupils who read both are counted twice.
